# Norovirus infection

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Norovirus infection*

[Original Article Link](/library/Gf0Bn2)

---

## Summary

<u>Noroviruses</u> are a frequent cause of <u>viral gastroenteritis</u> in individuals of all ages worldwide. Transmission commonly occurs from person to person, as well as through contact with contaminated surfaces, food, and water. The clinical presentation of <u>norovirus</u> infection includes acute-onset <u>vomiting</u> and <u>watery diarrhea</u>. If classic <u>clinical features of norovirus</u> are present, treatment can usually be given without diagnostic confirmation; however, viral studies are recommended in certain cases, e.g., <u>severe gastroenteritis</u>, suspected <u>outbreaks</u>. Treatment is typically supportive (e.g., <u>treatment of dehydration</u>) as the condition normally self-resolves within 72 hours. Given its <u>virulence</u> and short <u>incubation period</u>, <u>norovirus</u> infection may quickly lead to <u>outbreaks</u>, which must be reported.

---

## Epidemiology

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: November–March (winter months)

* Community <u>outbreaks</u> (in <u>nursing homes</u>, hospitals, preschools, cruise ships, etc.) are common.

* Older and <u>immunocompromised</u> patients are commonly affected.

* Most common cause of:

* Adult <u>gastroenteritis</u>

* Severe <u>acute gastroenteritis in children</u> younger than 5 years of age

* <u>Foodborne illness</u>





References:[[1]](/library/keam_j)[[2]](/library/leav_j)[[3]](/library/Nea-_j)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Norovirus</u>;  is a non‑enveloped <u>RNA</u> <u>calicivirus</u>.

* Transmission

* Fecal‑oral route through contaminated food or water, person‑to‑person contact, via airborne droplets, and contact with contaminated surfaces

* The <u>virus</u> is highly <u>virulent</u>.

* Individuals are highly infectious during the acute phase and 24–72 hours following onset of symptoms





> [!NOTE]
> Viral pathogens in <u>gastroenteritis</u> (<u>Rotavirus</u> is a <u>Reovirus</u>, <u>Norovirus</u> is a <u>Calicivirus</u>): Rotate Reo, the calico cat off to Norway!




References:[[4]](/library/5eaizj)

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Incubation period</u>: 12–48 hours

* <u>Nausea</u> and acute-onset <u>vomiting</u>

* Watery, nonbloody <u>diarrhea</u>

* Abdominal cramps

* <u>Fever</u>

* Symptoms resolve after 48–72 hours.

---

## Diagnosis

### Overview [[5]](/library/xMYEIp)[[6]](/library/J7Ys5q)




* Diagnosis is usually clinical; diagnostic studies are not required because confirmation does not affect management.

* Consider diagnostic studies in the following: [[5]](/library/xMYEIp)[[6]](/library/J7Ys5q)

* Patients with <u>red flags for diarrhea</u> or <u>risk factors</u> for severe infection

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Concern for community or institutional <u>outbreaks</u> (see “Prevention”)





> [!WARNING]
> Suspect a possible <u>norovirus</u> <u>outbreak</u> if ≥ 2 patients with an epidemiological link present with symptoms of <u>gastroenteritis</u> within the same timeframe. [[7]](/library/W41PRS0)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[3]](/library/Nea-_j)[[8]](/library/d41oRS0)[[9]](/library/541iPS0)




* Viral studies for <u>norovirus</u>: usually performed on whole stool   [[3]](/library/Nea-_j)

* Reverse <u>transcription</u>-<u>quantitative PCR</u> (<u>RT-qPCR</u>): preferred

* Multiplex assays: allow for detection of multiple pathogens

* Others (not routinely used in clinical practice): e.g., <u>enzyme immunoassays</u>, genotyping

* Additional studies

* Diagnostic uncertainty: Perform <u>diagnostic studies for infectious gastroenteritis</u>.

* <u>Signs of significant dehydration</u>: Perform <u>diagnostic studies for dehydration</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Whole stool is the preferred sample for viral testing. [[3]](/library/Nea-_j)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Rotavirus infection</u>

* <u>Bacterial gastroenteritis</u>

* <u>Food poisoning</u>





References:[[10]](/library/peaL-j)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

* Treatment is supportive (e.g., <u>fluid replacement</u>, <u>electrolyte repletion</u>, <u>antiemetics</u>). [[5]](/library/xMYEIp)[[6]](/library/J7Ys5q)[[11]](/library/CN1qWh0)

* Children: See “<u>Treatment of infectious gastroenteritis in children</u>.”

* Adults: See “<u>Supportive therapy for gastroenteritis</u>.”

* Patients with <u>severe gastroenteritis</u> or <u>signs of significant dehydration</u> may require inpatient treatment, including <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u>. [[5]](/library/xMYEIp)[[6]](/library/J7Ys5q)[[11]](/library/CN1qWh0)

* <u>Nitazoxanide</u> may reduce the duration of illness, but evidence supporting its use is limited.  [[12]](/library/Ij1YbS0)

* For outpatients, educate patients and/or caregivers on:

* The expected duration of illness

* <u>Return precautions</u>

* <u>Prevention of norovirus transmission</u>





> [!TIP]
> Adults aged > 65 years are at increased risk for complications (e.g., <u>dehydration</u>, prolonged symptom duration) and thus more likely to require hospital admission. [[13]](/library/1412RS0)
